en.title: Metallurgical and Materials Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What metallurgical and materials engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Metallurgical and materials engineering is the study of how materials are extracted, made, shaped, joined, treated and chosen for use. It covers metals and alloys, ceramics and glasses, polymers and composites. Metallurgy focuses on metals, from extraction and processing to structure and properties, while materials engineering looks at structure, properties, processing and performance for all material classes. The subject matters because a bridge, implant, pipe or engine part fails if its material is wrong or badly processed.

These notes teach principles. They do not replace standards, codes, laboratory rules or a registered engineer. Standards and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration. Check the current official source for any rule or limit.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree patterns differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BEng in metallurgical or materials engineering commonly takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES. Polytechnic students often take an ND, then supervised industrial work, then an HND. In the UK, a BEng commonly takes three years and an MEng four; Scottish courses often take one year longer. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own awards and durations.

Early years are usually shared with other engineering students: mathematics, chemistry, physics and mechanics. Later years add materials-specific subjects, laboratories, design or plant visits, and a final project. A master’s degree adds advanced theory, characterisation or modelling and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with foundations: engineering mathematics, general chemistry, physics, mechanics of materials, introduction to materials engineering, crystallography, material and energy balances, thermodynamics and kinetics, and laboratory measurement. These give the language for later work.

Core subjects then cover phase diagrams and transformations, diffusion, mechanical metallurgy, extractive metallurgy, ironmaking and steelmaking, steel heat treatment, nonferrous metallurgy, solidification and casting, metal forming and additive manufacturing, welding and joining, ceramics and glasses, polymers and composites, corrosion, characterisation, failure analysis and non-destructive testing, materials selection and design, and professional practice, ethics and registration.

Master’s level adds advanced thermodynamics and phase equilibria, computational materials modelling, advanced characterisation and electron microscopy, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study with a pen and a calculator. Draw the structure, phase diagram or free-body diagram before writing equations. Write units on every line and check whether the answer is reasonable. Learn to read phase diagrams and cooling curves slowly, because many later topics depend on them. Keep a laboratory notebook that records method, readings, units and errors. Learn safety rules before entering a workshop or laboratory.

Use software after you can do a simple hand calculation, and check its output against that calculation. Practise past questions and explain each term in your own words. Visit plants or workshops when you can, because they show how ore, melt, heat treatment and inspection fit together.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Common mistakes include mixing units, confusing stress with strain, and using a value from a table without checking its conditions. Students often read a phase diagram as if equilibrium always applies, forgetting cooling rate and kinetics. Heat treatment terms such as annealing, normalising, quenching and tempering are sometimes used loosely; learn what each does to structure and properties.

Do not copy a code clause or standard limit without checking the current edition and the country it applies to. Do not treat software output as correct because it looks precise. In laboratories, ignoring safety or recording readings without units can ruin a report. State assumptions clearly, as an examiner and a future employer need to see how you reached the answer.

keyPoints: Metallurgical and materials engineering links extraction, processing, structure, properties and performance.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Standards, codes and registration differ by country; COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria.
Learn phase diagrams, units and diagrams before trusting software.
Laboratory safety and a clear notebook are part of the subject, not extras.
State assumptions and check that every answer is reasonable.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for materials engineers
en.short: Functions, calculus, vectors, matrices, complex numbers and first-order ODEs applied to materials.

sections.heading: Functions and calculus
sections.text: A function maps each input to one output; for example, temperature T(t) during cooling is a function of time. The derivative dT/dt is the instantaneous rate of change, so a negative value means cooling. The chain rule handles nested relations such as C(x(t)). The concentration gradient dC/dx drives diffusion: Fick’s first law is J = −D dC/dx, where J is flux, D is diffusivity and the minus sign shows flow down the gradient. Differentiation also finds maxima and minima.

sections.heading: Integration and ODEs
sections.text: Integration reverses differentiation and adds up small contributions. The area under a cooling curve is ∫T dt, and the area under a flux curve gives the mass transferred per unit area. A first-order differential equation relates a quantity to its rate of change; separation of variables can solve it. Newton’s law of cooling, dT/dt = −k(T − T∞), has solution T = T∞ + (T0 − T∞)e^(−kt), where T∞ is surrounding temperature and k is a rate constant. Example: T0 = 100 °C, T∞ = 25 °C, k = 0.02 min⁻¹, t = 50 min. Then e^(−1) = 0.368, so T = 25 + 75 × 0.368 = 52.6 °C.

sections.heading: Vectors and matrices
sections.text: A vector has magnitude and direction; a temperature gradient is a vector. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Matrix multiplication combines linear equations, such as mass balances: A x = b, where x holds unknown stream masses. Solving by elimination or an inverse gives x. Simple balance: 100 kg feed splits so x = 3y. Then 3y + y = 100, so y = 25 kg and x = 75 kg.

sections.heading: Complex numbers
sections.text: Complex numbers have form a + bi, where i² = −1. They arise when solving x² + 1 = 0 and in AC impedance measurements, where impedance has real and imaginary parts. Addition is componentwise; multiplication uses i² = −1. The modulus |a + bi| = √(a² + b²) gives magnitude.

keyPoints: The derivative dT/dt gives the instantaneous rate of change; for cooling it is negative.
Fick’s first law J = −D dC/dx shows flux down a concentration gradient.
Newton’s law of cooling dT/dt = −k(T − T∞) solves to T = T∞ + (T0 − T∞)e^(−kt).
Integration adds small contributions and gives areas under curves, such as mass transferred per unit area from flux.
A matrix equation A x = b represents linked mass balances and is solved by elimination or an inverse.
Complex numbers a + bi, with i² = −1, have modulus √(a² + b²) and appear in AC impedance.

en.title: General chemistry for materials
en.short: Atomic structure, bonding, moles, solutions, acids, bases, redox and equilibrium for materials.

sections.heading: Atoms and bonding
sections.text:
An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. Atomic number Z is the number of protons and fixes the element; isotopes have equal Z but different neutrons. Valence electrons, in the outer shell, control bonding. The periodic table lists elements by increasing Z. A group is a column with similar valence electrons; a period is a row. Across a period atomic radius generally falls and electronegativity rises; down a group radius rises. Electronegativity is the tendency to attract shared electrons.

Metals bond metallically: positive ions in a lattice with delocalised electrons. This gives conduction and ductility. Ceramics are mainly ionic or covalent. Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction after electron transfer; covalent bonding is sharing electron pairs. Ionic solids are hard and brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved. Covalent solids are often hard and insulating.

sections.heading: Moles and solutions
sections.text:
Stoichiometry relates amounts through a balanced equation. One mole contains Avogadro’s number of particles, about 6.022 × 10²³. Molar mass is grams per mole. For solutions, concentration c = n ÷ V, with n in mol and V in dm³ (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³).

Example: 5.00 g NaOH (M = 40.00 g/mol) made to 250 cm³ gives
n = 5.00 ÷ 40.00 = 0.125 mol
c = 0.125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.500 mol/dm³.
Reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium when forward and reverse rates are equal; K is the ratio of product to reactant activities at a given temperature.

sections.heading: Acids, bases, redox
sections.text:
An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. pH = −log10[H⁺]; at 25 °C neutral pH is 7.

In redox, oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain. Corrosion couples an anodic metal reaction, M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻, to a cathodic reaction such as oxygen reduction. In an electrochemical cell the anode is where oxidation occurs and the cathode where reduction occurs. Ceramics usually lack free electrons, so they are poor conductors.

keyPoints: Atomic number Z is the proton count and fixes the element; valence electrons control bonding.
Metallic bonding gives delocalised electrons, so metals conduct and deform; ionic and covalent ceramics are usually harder and less conductive.
Amount in moles n = mass ÷ molar mass, and one mole contains about 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
Solution concentration c = n ÷ V, with V in dm³; 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
pH = −log10[H⁺]; at 25 °C neutral pH is 7.
Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain; at equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal.

en.title: Physics for materials
en.short: Force, energy, heat transfer, elastic waves and electrical conduction for materials.

sections.heading: Force and energy
sections.text:
Force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). Work is force times distance along the force, W = Fd, in joules (J). Energy is capacity to do work, also in J. Power is energy per second, P = E/t, in watts (W). A mass m moving at speed v has kinetic energy ½mv².

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s has ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. Always convert to SI units before calculating: 1 kN = 1000 N and 1 mm = 0.001 m. In materials, forces move dislocations and break bonds, while energy changes explain heating and deformation.

sections.heading: Heat transfer
sections.text:
Temperature measures average thermal energy per particle, in kelvin (K). Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, in J. In solids, conduction is the main mode. The Fourier law gives the rate: Q/t = kAΔT/L, where k is thermal conductivity in W/(m·K), A is area, ΔT is temperature difference and L is thickness.

Example: k = 50 W/(m·K), A = 0.02 m², ΔT = 100 K, L = 0.10 m. Then Q/t = 50 × 0.02 × 100 ÷ 0.10 = 1000 W. Metals have high k because free electrons carry heat; polymers and ceramics have lower k.

sections.heading: Waves and conduction
sections.text:
An elastic wave is a disturbance travelling through a material by elastic deformation. In a thin rod, the longitudinal wave speed is v = √(E/ρ), where E is elastic modulus in Pa and ρ is density in kg/m³.

Example: E = 70 GPa = 70 × 10⁹ Pa and ρ = 2700 kg/m³. v = √(70 × 10⁹ ÷ 2700) = √(2.59 × 10⁷) = 5.09 × 10³ m/s.

Electrical conduction: current I in amperes (A) is charge flow rate. Ohm’s law is V = IR. Resistance is R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity in Ω·m. Conductivity is σ = 1/ρ. Example: a copper wire with L = 2 m, A = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² and ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m has R = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 2 ÷ (1 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.034 Ω. Metals conduct well because free electrons move; ceramics and polymers conduct poorly.

keyPoints: Work is W = Fd and kinetic energy is ½mv²; both are in joules.
Power is P = E/t in watts; convert kN to N and mm to m before calculating.
Conduction rate is Q/t = kAΔT/L, with k in W/(m·K).
Longitudinal elastic wave speed in a thin rod is v = √(E/ρ).
Resistance is R = ρL/A and Ohm’s law is V = IR; conductivity σ = 1/ρ.
Metals usually conduct heat and electricity well because free electrons carry both.

en.title: Mechanics of materials: stress, strain and simple members
en.short: Stress, strain, Hooke’s law, axial, bending and torsion formulas, and simple failure checks.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text:
Stress σ is force per area, in N/mm² or MPa. Strain ε is change in length divided by original length and has no units. In the elastic range Hooke’s law gives σ = Eε, where E is Young’s modulus.

Other elastic constants are shear modulus G, bulk modulus K and Poisson’s ratio ν, the ratio of lateral to axial strain. For an isotropic material G = E/[2(1+ν)]. Elastic means deformation recovers.

sections.heading: Axial loading
sections.text:
A bar under axial force F deforms by δ = FL/(AE), where L is length and A is cross-sectional area. The internal force comes from equilibrium.

Stress is σ = F/A when the load acts through the centroid and away from the ends. Example: steel rod, d = 20 mm, L = 2 m, F = 50 kN, E = 200 GPa. A = πd²/4 = 314.2 mm². σ = 50,000 ÷ 314.2 = 159 MPa. δ = 50,000 × 2,000 ÷ (314.2 × 200,000) = 1.59 mm.

sections.heading: Bending and torsion
sections.text:
For a beam bent by moment M, σ = My/I, where I is the second moment of area and y is distance from the neutral axis (where stress is zero). For a rectangle b × d, I = bd³/12.

Example: b = 50 mm, d = 100 mm, M = 2 kN·m. I = 50 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 4.167 × 10⁶ mm⁴. ymax = 50 mm. σ = 2 × 10⁶ × 50 ÷ 4.167 × 10⁶ = 24 N/mm². A solid circular shaft under torque T has shear stress τ = Tr/J and twist θ = TL/(GJ), where r is the radius and J is the polar second moment of area, equal to πd⁴/32.

sections.heading: Failure criteria
sections.text:
Yielding begins when stress reaches yield strength; fracture may follow at ultimate strength. Design rule is factor of safety = failure stress ÷ allowable stress.

Codes and safety factors differ by country and application, so check current local code. Ductile metals are checked against yield using von Mises or Tresca criterion; brittle materials against principal stress.

keyPoints: Stress is force per area; strain is change in length divided by original length.
Hooke’s law in the elastic range: σ = Eε, with E Young’s modulus.
Axial deformation: δ = FL/(AE), and stress σ = F/A.
Bending stress: σ = My/I; for a rectangle I = bd³/12.
Torsion of a solid circular shaft: τ = Tr/J and θ = TL/(GJ), with J = πd⁴/32.
Factor of safety = failure stress ÷ allowable stress; design codes and safety factors vary by country, so check the local code.

en.title: Introduction to materials engineering
en.short: The five material classes, structure across scales, properties, uses and how engineers choose materials.

sections.heading: Classes of materials
sections.text: Materials are substances chosen to make products. Engineers group them into five broad classes. Metals conduct heat and electricity, are strong and can deform permanently without breaking; examples include steel for structures and copper for wires. Ceramics are hard, stiff and heat resistant but brittle; examples include bricks, cutting tools and electrical insulators. Polymers are light, flexible and often cheap, with low heat conduction; examples include pipes, packaging and casings. Composites combine two or more materials, such as glass fibres in a polymer, to gain stiffness at low mass. Semiconductors conduct poorly compared with metals, but their conductivity can be controlled precisely, so they are used in chips and sensors. Each class covers a range of properties, so no class is best for every use.

sections.heading: Structure to performance
sections.text: The central idea is processing-structure-properties-performance. Structure is the arrangement of atoms and bonds, grains, pores and fibres, and visible features, at atomic, microscopic and macroscopic scales. Processing, such as casting, forming or heat treatment, changes that arrangement. Structure sets properties, which are measurable behaviours such as strength, stiffness, density, conductivity and corrosion resistance. Properties then decide performance in service. For example, two steel bars of the same composition can behave differently after different heat treatments because their internal structure differs. Engineers therefore cannot choose a material from its name alone; they must know how it will be made and used.

sections.heading: Choosing a material
sections.text: Selection starts from function and constraints: loads, temperature, environment, mass, cost and manufacture. Engineers compare candidate materials by properties, then check form, joining, availability and local standards. Codes and standards differ by country, so check the current national code or approved equivalent. A small case: a Lagos bicycle workshop may choose steel for a low-cost frame because it is stiff, easy to weld and repairable, though heavier than aluminium. A material that looks best on paper may fail if it cannot be made or repaired locally.

keyPoints: Metals, ceramics, polymers, composites and semiconductors are the main classes of engineering materials.
Each class covers a range of properties, so no class is best for every application.
Processing-structure-properties-performance links how a material is made to how it behaves in service.
Structure at atomic, microscopic and macroscopic scales controls strength, stiffness, conductivity and other properties.
Materials selection balances function, constraints, cost, manufacture, availability and local codes.
Codes and standards differ by country, so check the current national code or approved equivalent.

en.title: Crystallography and crystal structure
en.short: Lattices, unit cells, Miller indices, packing and common metal and ceramic structures.

sections.heading: Lattices and unit cells
sections.text:
A crystal lattice is a regular array of points. The unit cell is the repeating box defined by edge lengths a, b, c and angles α, β, γ. A Bravais lattice is one of the 14 distinct point arrays in three dimensions; the seven crystal systems group them by cell shape.

Placing a basis of atoms on each lattice point gives the crystal structure. Common metallic structures are face-centred cubic (FCC), body-centred cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP); simple cubic (SC) is rare among metals but is the simplest case.

sections.heading: Indexing planes and directions
sections.text:
For a plane, find its intercepts on the axes in units of a, b, c, take reciprocals, clear fractions and write (hkl). A negative index takes a bar. For a direction, subtract tail coordinates from head coordinates, reduce to smallest integers and write [uvw]. Families are {hkl} and <uvw>.

To draw a plane, mark the intercepts and join them; intercepts 1, ∞, ∞ give (100).

sections.heading: Packing and density
sections.text:
Atomic packing factor (APF) is volume of atoms in the cell divided by cell volume, for hard spheres. APF is 0.52 for SC, 0.68 for BCC and 0.74 for FCC and HCP. Theoretical density is ρ = n M ÷ (N_A V), where n is atoms per cell, M molar mass, N_A Avogadro constant and V cell volume.

Example: copper is FCC, a = 0.361 nm, M = 0.06355 kg/mol, n = 4. V = (0.361 × 10⁻⁹)³ = 4.70 × 10⁻²⁹ m³. ρ = 4 × 0.06355 ÷ (6.022 × 10²³ × 4.70 × 10⁻²⁹) = 8.98 × 10³ kg/m³.

sections.heading: Structures and slip
sections.text:
Metals often adopt FCC (Al, Cu, γ-Fe), BCC (α-Fe, W) or HCP (Mg, Zn, α-Ti). Ceramics are compounds: NaCl has FCC Cl⁻ with Na⁺ in octahedral holes; CsCl has a two-atom simple-cubic basis; CaF₂ is fluorite; ABO₃ is perovskite.

Slip occurs on the most densely packed planes and directions, so FCC has 12 {111}<110> systems, BCC has many, and HCP has few at room temperature.

keyPoints: Miller planes use reciprocals of axial intercepts in (hkl); directions use reduced vector components in [uvw].
APF = volume of atoms ÷ cell volume: 0.52 for SC, 0.68 for BCC, 0.74 for FCC and HCP.
Theoretical density: ρ = n M ÷ (N_A V), with M in kg/mol and V in m³.
FCC metals slip on 12 {111}<110> systems; HCP metals have fewer slip systems at room temperature.
Common metal structures are FCC, BCC and HCP; ceramic structures include rock salt, CsCl, fluorite and perovskite.
There are 14 Bravais lattices in three dimensions, grouped into seven crystal systems.

en.title: Material and energy balances
en.short: Mass and energy balances: stoichiometry, recycle and bypass, and simple heat balances.

sections.heading: Balance principles
sections.text: A material balance accounts for mass entering, leaving, accumulating and reacting in a system. At steady state, accumulation is zero: input = output + consumption for a reactant, or input + generation = output for a product. Choose a basis, such as 1 hour or 100 kg feed, and use consistent units: kg, kmol, s, kJ, K. Convert all flows to the same time unit before adding them. For a compound, work in moles so stoichiometric coefficients can be used directly.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry and recycle
sections.text:
Stoichiometry gives the mole ratio in which substances react. For aA + bB -> cC, one kmol of A needs b/a kmol of B. A recycle stream returns unreacted material to the reactor; a bypass sends part of the feed around a unit; a purge removes a small stream to stop inert material building up. Solve recycle problems with two balances: one around the whole process and one around the reactor.

Example: fresh feed 100 kg/h contains 20 kg/h A and 80 kg/h inert. Per-pass conversion of A is 50%, and all unreacted A recycles. Overall A reacted = 20 kg/h. Let recycle = R. A entering reactor = 20 + R; reacted = 0.5(20 + R) = 20, so R = 20 kg/h. Check: A leaving reactor = 20 kg/h, which is recycled.

sections.heading: Heat balances
sections.text:
An energy balance follows the same pattern: energy in = energy out + accumulation + losses. For a stream heated without reaction, sensible heat is Q = m cp ΔT, where m is mass flow, cp is specific heat capacity and ΔT is the temperature change. Use kJ, kg, K and kW (kJ/s). Add latent heat for melting or vaporisation.

Example: 2 kg/s of material with cp = 0.5 kJ/(kg·K) heated from 25 °C to 125 °C: Q = 2 × 0.5 × (125 − 25) = 100 kW.

sections.heading: Checking results
sections.text: Check that every stream’s units match, that mass and moles close, and that temperature differences use K or °C consistently. A balance that does not close means a stream, reaction or unit conversion was missed.

keyPoints: At steady state, mass in = mass out plus consumption, or mass in plus generation = mass out.
Choose a basis and convert every flow to the same units before calculating.
For aA + bB -> cC, the mole ratio is b/a kmol B per kmol A.
Recycle returns unreacted material; bypass skips a unit; purge prevents inert buildup.
Sensible heat: Q = m cp ΔT, with m in kg/s, cp in kJ/(kg·K), ΔT in K and Q in kW.
Check that mass and moles close and that units are consistent.

en.title: Thermodynamics and kinetics: foundations
en.short: The first, second and third laws, enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy, phase equilibrium and reaction kinetics.

sections.heading: Energy and enthalpy
sections.text: The first law says energy is conserved. For a closed system, ΔU = q − w, where U is internal energy, q is heat added to the system and w is work done by the system. Enthalpy H = U + PV. At constant pressure, q = ΔH, so enthalpy is the heat exchanged in many metallurgical processes. A negative ΔH means heat is released (exothermic); positive means absorbed (endothermic).

sections.heading: Entropy and Gibbs energy
sections.text: The second law says the total entropy S of an isolated system cannot decrease. Entropy measures energy dispersal. A process is spontaneous only if total entropy rises. The third law says a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K. Gibbs energy G = H − TS combines them. At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔG < 0 the reaction or phase change is spontaneous; if ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium. Example: ΔH = −100 kJ/mol, ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K), T = 298 K. TΔS = 298 × (−0.200) = −59.6 kJ/mol. ΔG = −100 − (−59.6) = −40.4 kJ/mol, so the reaction is spontaneous.

sections.heading: Phase equilibrium
sections.text: A phase change occurs when one phase has lower Gibbs energy. At equilibrium the two phases have equal Gibbs energy, so ΔG = 0; this fixes the melting point or boiling point at a given pressure. In alloys, equilibrium between phases also requires equal chemical potential of each component, where the chemical potential of a component is its partial molar Gibbs energy in that phase.

sections.heading: Reaction kinetics
sections.text: Kinetics tells how fast a reaction goes. A simple rate law for one reactant is rate = k[A]^n, where k is the rate constant and n is the order. The Arrhenius equation k = A exp(−Ea/RT), where A is the pre-exponential factor and R is the gas constant, shows rate rises with temperature. Ea is the activation energy, the energy barrier reactants must overcome. A catalyst lowers Ea without changing ΔG. Thermodynamics says whether a change is possible; kinetics says whether it is fast enough.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: ΔU = q − w, with w done by the system.
Enthalpy is H = U + PV; at constant pressure q = ΔH.
Second law: total entropy cannot decrease; third law: a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K.
Gibbs energy is G = H − TS; at constant T and P, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and ΔG < 0 means spontaneous.
At phase equilibrium ΔG = 0 and the chemical potentials of each component are equal.
Arrhenius equation: k = A exp(−Ea/RT); for a simple rate law, rate = k[A]^n.

en.title: Materials laboratory and measurement
en.short: Covers lab safety, uncertainty, tensile and hardness tests, sample preparation, microscopy and reporting.

sections.heading: Safety and planning
sections.text:
Before any test, read the risk assessment and your institution’s safety rules. Wear eye protection and keep solvents away from flames. Handle acids in a fume hood with gloves. Know the emergency stop and spill kit.

Plan in writing: aim, variables, specimen, equipment, procedure and safety. Calibrate instruments. Record raw readings immediately with date, sample identity and instrument number.

sections.heading: Measurement and error
sections.text:
Every measurement has uncertainty. Resolution is the smallest scale change. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Repeat readings reduce random error; calibration reduces systematic error.

For n readings, s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)) and the standard uncertainty of the mean is u = s ÷ √n.

Example: readings 10.02, 10.04, 10.00, 10.02, 10.02 mm. Mean = 10.02 mm. Σ(x − x̄)² = 0.0008 mm². s = √(0.0008 ÷ 4) = 0.014 mm. u = 0.014 ÷ √5 = 0.006 mm. Round the uncertainty to the same decimal place as the readings, so report 10.02 ± 0.01 mm.

sections.heading: Tensile and hardness
sections.text:
A tensile test pulls a specimen at a controlled rate and records force F and extension ΔL. Engineering stress σ = F ÷ A0, where A0 is original area. Strain ε = ΔL ÷ L0. The curve gives yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation.

Example: F = 10.0 kN on a 5.00 mm diameter specimen. A0 = π × 5.00² ÷ 4 = 19.63 mm². σ = 10,000 ÷ 19.63 = 509 N/mm².

Hardness presses an indenter into the surface. Brinell uses a ball and indentation diameter; Vickers uses a diamond pyramid and diagonals; Rockwell uses depth. Report method, load and scale.

sections.heading: Microscopy and reporting
sections.text:
For microscopy, cut a section, mount, grind with finer papers, polish and etch if needed. Record magnification and a scale bar.

A report has title, aim, method, results with units and uncertainty, discussion and conclusion. Show one worked calculation and compare with expected values. Standards differ by country; cite the edition and check the current official source.

keyPoints: Plan safety, calibration and raw data recording before starting a test.
Stress = force ÷ original area; strain = extension ÷ original length.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)); uncertainty of the mean = s ÷ √n.
Report every result with units and an uncertainty, and show one worked calculation.
Hardness values depend on method, load and scale, so state all three.
Standards and codes differ by country; cite the edition you used and check the current official source.

en.title: Phase diagrams and phase transformations
en.short: Binary phase diagrams, lever rule, eutectic, eutectoid, peritectic, and nucleation and growth.

sections.heading: Reading diagrams
sections.text: A binary phase diagram plots temperature against composition for two components at fixed pressure. Single-phase regions show one solid or liquid solution. Two-phase regions show a mixture; a tie line at the chosen temperature gives the compositions of the two phases at its ends. The liquidus marks all-liquid above; the solidus marks all-solid below. Read composition horizontally and temperature vertically.

sections.heading: Lever rule
sections.text:
The lever rule gives phase fractions in a two-phase region. For alloy C0 with tie-line ends Cα and Cβ, fraction α = (Cβ − C0) ÷ (Cβ − Cα) and fraction β = (C0 − Cα) ÷ (Cβ − Cα).

Example: C0 = 40 wt% B, Cα = 20 wt% B, Cβ = 70 wt% B. Fraction α = (70 − 40) ÷ (70 − 20) = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60. Fraction β = (40 − 20) ÷ 50 = 0.40. The alloy is 60% α and 40% β by mass.

sections.heading: Invariant reactions
sections.text: Three important reactions at fixed temperature appear as horizontal lines. Eutectic: on cooling, a liquid of fixed composition transforms into two solids, L → α + β. Eutectoid: a solid transforms into two solids, γ → α + β. Peritectic: a liquid and a solid form a new solid, L + α → β. Eutectic and eutectoid differ in the parent phase. A peritectic often stalls because the new solid separates the reactants.

sections.heading: Nucleation and growth
sections.text: Below the solidus, phases change by nucleation and growth. Nucleation is the formation of small stable particles of a new phase; it is easier at grain boundaries and defects (heterogeneous) than inside grains (homogeneous). Growth moves the interface as atoms diffuse. Temperature and time control the result: low temperature gives many nuclei but slow growth; high temperature gives few nuclei but fast growth. Phase diagrams give equilibrium phases; heat treatment uses controlled cooling and holding to reach microstructures that can differ from equilibrium.

keyPoints: A tie line at a chosen temperature gives the compositions of the two phases in equilibrium.
Lever rule: fraction α = (Cβ − C0) ÷ (Cβ − Cα) and fraction β = (C0 − Cα) ÷ (Cβ − Cα).
Eutectic: L → α + β; eutectoid: γ → α + β; peritectic: L + α → β.
Phase diagrams show equilibrium; real microstructures depend on cooling rate and time.
Solid-state transformations occur by nucleation and growth, with nucleation favoured at defects and growth favoured by diffusion at higher temperature.
Use wt% or at% consistently: the lever rule gives mass fractions for wt% and atom fractions for at%.

en.title: Diffusion in solids: laws, mechanisms and applications
en.short: Fick’s laws, diffusion mechanisms, temperature dependence, and applications such as carburising and sintering.

sections.heading: Fick’s first law
sections.text: Diffusion is the movement of atoms through a material because of a concentration gradient. Fick’s first law describes steady state: J = −D dC/dx. J is flux (mol m⁻² s⁻¹ or kg m⁻² s⁻¹), C is concentration, x is distance and D is the diffusion coefficient (m² s⁻¹). The minus sign shows flow from high to low concentration. D measures how quickly a gradient is smoothed; it depends on species, host, path and temperature.

sections.heading: Second law and solutions
sections.text: When concentration changes with time, Fick’s second law applies: ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x² for constant D. It balances concentration change in a small volume against flux entering and leaving. For a semi-infinite solid with fixed surface concentration, C(x,t) = C0 + (Cs − C0)[1 − erf(x ÷ (2√(Dt)))], where erf is the error function. This underlies carburising calculations. The term √(Dt) has units of length and sets the diffusion distance.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and temperature
sections.text: Atoms move by mechanisms. Interstitial diffusion is small atoms such as carbon moving between lattice sites; it is fast. Substitutional diffusion needs vacancies, so it is slower. Grain boundary and surface diffusion are faster than bulk but carry less material. Temperature acts through the Arrhenius equation: D = D0 exp(−Q ÷ RT), where D0 is a pre-exponential factor, Q activation energy, R the gas constant and T absolute temperature. Higher T or lower Q gives larger D.

sections.heading: Applications and example
sections.text: Carburising uses interstitial carbon diffusion into steel at high temperature to raise surface carbon. Sintering joins powder particles as vacancies diffuse away from necks. Homogenisation reduces segregation by letting solute diffuse. Example: steady-state diffusion through a 2 mm plate with D = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² m² s⁻¹ and concentration difference 0.8 kg m⁻³. J = D ΔC ÷ Δx = (2.0 × 10⁻¹²)(0.8) ÷ 0.002 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. Units check: m² s⁻¹ × kg m⁻³ ÷ m = kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

keyPoints: Fick’s first law for steady state is J = −D dC/dx.
Fick’s second law is ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x² when D is constant.
D has units m² s⁻¹ and measures how quickly a concentration gradient is smoothed.
Temperature dependence follows D = D0 exp(−Q ÷ RT).
Interstitial diffusion is faster than substitutional diffusion, which needs vacancies.
Carburising, sintering and homogenisation are industrial uses of solid-state diffusion.

en.title: Mechanical metallurgy: plastic deformation, fracture and creep
en.short: Slip, twinning, dislocations, strengthening, fracture, fatigue and creep in metals.

sections.heading: Plastic deformation
sections.text: Plastic deformation is permanent shape change after yield. On a stress-strain curve, yield begins plastic flow and the peak is tensile strength. In metals, flow occurs mainly by slip: dislocations glide on close-packed planes in close-packed directions. Resolved shear stress is τ = σ cos φ cos λ, where φ is the angle between load axis and slip plane normal, and λ is the angle between axis and slip direction. Twinning shears a region into a mirror orientation when slip is difficult. Example: σ = 100 MPa, φ = λ = 45°, so τ = 100 × 0.707 × 0.707 = 50 MPa.

sections.heading: Dislocations and strengthening
sections.text: Dislocations are line defects; their motion produces slip. Strength rises when dislocation motion is blocked. Grain boundaries hinder slip: Hall-Petch gives σy = σ0 + k ÷ √d, where d is grain size. Solid-solution atoms, precipitates and other dislocations also obstruct motion. Strain hardening comes from dislocation multiplication. Ductility generally falls as strength rises, so strengthening is a trade-off. Microstructure sets the balance.

sections.heading: Fracture and fatigue
sections.text: Fracture is separation of material. Ductile fracture involves plastic flow and dimples; brittle fracture is fast, with little deformation. Fracture toughness KIC measures resistance to crack growth; small flaws matter more when toughness is low. Fatigue is failure under repeated stress, even below yield. A fatigue test plots stress amplitude S against cycles to failure N, giving an S-N curve. Cracks start at stress concentrations and grow. Steels often show an endurance limit, a stress amplitude below which they do not fail; many nonferrous alloys do not. Design uses safe stress ranges.

sections.heading: Creep
sections.text: Creep is time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained load, important at high temperature, often above 0.4 of the absolute melting temperature. A creep curve has primary, secondary and tertiary stages; secondary creep is slowest and steady. Mechanisms include diffusion and dislocation climb. Creep strength falls as temperature or stress rises. Tests record strain against time at constant stress and temperature. Design uses allowable limits from standards, which differ by country.

keyPoints: Slip is dislocation glide on close-packed planes and directions; resolved shear stress is τ = σ cos φ cos λ.
Twinning reorients a region by shear and can operate when slip is restricted.
Hall-Petch: σy = σ0 + k ÷ √d, so finer grains raise yield strength.
Solid solution, precipitates, grain boundaries and strain hardening obstruct dislocations, raising strength but often lowering ductility.
Ductile fracture shows plastic flow, brittle fracture shows little, and low fracture toughness makes small cracks dangerous.
Fatigue is repeated-stress failure below yield, shown by S-N curves, while creep is time-dependent deformation at high temperature.

en.title: Extractive metallurgy: from ore to metal
en.short: From ore to metal: liberation, concentration, roasting, smelting, leaching and electrowinning.

sections.heading: Ore to concentrate
sections.text: An ore is rock containing a valuable mineral in a concentration worth working. The unwanted rock is gangue. Mineral processing liberates valuable grains by crushing and grinding, then concentrates them. Liberation means grinding until most valuable grains are exposed. Concentration separates grains by a physical property: density in gravity separation, magnetism in magnetic separation, or surface wettability in froth flotation. The product is a concentrate; the residue is tailings.

sections.heading: Pyrometallurgy
sections.text: Pyrometallurgy uses heat. Roasting heats a concentrate in air, usually to oxidise sulphides and remove sulphur or volatile oxides. Smelting melts concentrate with a flux (a slag-forming additive) and often a reducing agent such as coke, forming a metal, matte (a metal sulphide melt) or slag. Slag is molten oxide waste carrying gangue. Converting removes sulphur or carbon from molten metal or matte. A reaction runs if its overall Gibbs energy change is negative at furnace temperature. Furnaces need fuel or electrical heat and off-gas cleaning.

sections.heading: Hydrometallurgy
sections.text: Hydrometallurgy dissolves the metal. Leaching contacts ore or concentrate with a reagent that selectively dissolves the valuable metal, leaving gangue. Acid, alkali, chloride or cyanide solutions are common; choice depends on metal and host mineral. The metal-bearing leach solution is purified by solvent extraction, ion exchange or precipitation, then recovered by electrowinning or chemical reduction.

sections.heading: Electrometallurgy
sections.text:
Electrometallurgy uses electrical energy. In electrowinning, current reduces dissolved metal ions at the cathode: Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻ → M. Electrorefining purifies an impure anode by the same principle. Faraday’s law gives m = MIt ÷ (nF), where M is molar mass, I current, t time, n electrons per ion, F = 96,485 C/mol. Example: copper, M = 63.55 g/mol, n = 2, I = 10,000 A, t = 86,400 s, efficiency 95%.
Charge = 10,000 × 86,400 = 8.64 × 10⁸ C
m = 63.55 × 8.64 × 10⁸ ÷ (2 × 96,485) = 284.5 kg
At 95%: 0.95 × 284.5 = 270.3 kg.
Energy and reagent costs help decide the route.

keyPoints: Mineral processing liberates and concentrates valuable minerals before extraction.
Roasting and smelting use heat; slag removes gangue and matte may form.
Leaching dissolves metal selectively; purification precedes recovery.
Electrowinning reduces metal ions at the cathode using electrical current.
Faraday’s law: m = MIt ÷ (nF), with F = 96,485 C/mol.
Route choice depends on ore mineralogy, reagent and energy costs, and environmental control.

en.title: Ironmaking and steelmaking
en.short: Blast furnace ironmaking, basic oxygen and electric arc steelmaking, refining, casting and alloy types.

sections.heading: Blast furnace
sections.text:
In the blast furnace, iron ore, coke and limestone are charged at the top. Hot air blown through nozzles called tuyeres burns coke to carbon dioxide, which reacts with more coke to give carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide reduces the ore:

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2

Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which combines with silica and alumina to form slag (molten waste). Molten iron absorbs carbon and sinks; slag floats and is tapped separately. The product is hot metal, or pig iron, high in carbon.

sections.heading: Steelmaking routes
sections.text:
Steelmaking lowers carbon and oxidises silicon, manganese and phosphorus; sulphur is removed to the slag. In basic oxygen steelmaking, oxygen is blown onto molten hot metal with scrap and lime flux. Carbon leaves as carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide; lime forms a basic slag that takes up phosphorus and sulphur. The reaction is exothermic.

In the electric arc furnace, scrap or direct-reduced iron is melted by an electric arc, then refined. It suits alloy steels and recycling. Both routes produce liquid steel.

sections.heading: Refining and casting
sections.text:
Secondary metallurgy in a ladle adjusts composition and temperature. Deoxidation removes dissolved oxygen with aluminium, silicon or manganese; the oxides form inclusions, which may float into the slag. Aluminium forms alumina particles. Degassing removes hydrogen and nitrogen under vacuum. The steel is then cast.

Continuous casting pours steel through a water-cooled mould to form a solid shell, then into slabs, blooms or billets. Ingot casting remains for some large forgings. Solidification can cause segregation, so casting conditions matter.

sections.heading: Cast iron and steel
sections.text:
Cast iron has more carbon than steel; its brittleness depends on graphite shape. Grey iron has flake graphite and good damping; white iron has cementite (iron carbide) and is hard and wear-resistant; ductile iron has nodular graphite from magnesium treatment; malleable iron is heat-treated white iron.

Steels include plain carbon (low, medium and high carbon), low-alloy steels for strength, stainless steels with chromium for corrosion resistance, and tool steels for hardness. Heat treatment and alloying set the final properties.

keyPoints: The blast furnace reduces iron ore with carbon monoxide, Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, and removes impurities as slag.
Basic oxygen steelmaking blows oxygen onto hot metal with lime flux; the electric arc furnace melts scrap or direct-reduced iron.
Secondary metallurgy adjusts composition; deoxidation forms oxide inclusions that should float into the slag.
Continuous casting solidifies steel into slabs, blooms or billets, while ingot casting remains for some large forgings.
Cast irons differ by graphite shape: grey flake, white cementite, ductile nodular and malleable heat-treated.
Steels range from plain carbon to low-alloy, stainless and tool steels, with properties set by alloying and heat treatment.

en.title: Steel heat treatment and property control
en.short: Annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering, austempering, surface hardening and hardenability.

sections.heading: Transformations and cooling
sections.text: Heat treatment controls austenite transformation. On the iron-carbon diagram, the eutectoid is about 0.8% carbon at about 727 °C. Slow cooling gives coarse pearlite; faster cooling gives fine pearlite; very fast cooling suppresses diffusion and gives martensite. TTT diagrams show isothermal transformation and CCT diagrams show continuous cooling. The critical cooling rate is the slowest rate that avoids pearlite and bainite. Hardenability is the depth to which a steel hardens; it depends on composition and grain size. The Jominy end-quench test compares hardenability.

sections.heading: Annealing and normalising
sections.text: Annealing heats, holds and cools slowly, usually in the furnace. It softens, relieves stress and refines grain. Spheroidising, for high-carbon steels, makes cementite spheroids and improves machinability. Normalising heats above the upper critical temperature and cools in air. It gives finer pearlite than annealing, so it is stronger and harder, and it refines grain.

sections.heading: Hardening, tempering, surfaces
sections.text: Hardening austenitises and quenches fast enough to form martensite, which is hard but brittle. Tempering reheats below the lower critical temperature: low temperature keeps wear resistance, higher temperature gives toughness. Austempering quenches into a bath above the martensite start temperature and holds until bainite forms, reducing distortion. Surface hardening keeps a tough core: carburising adds carbon before quenching, nitriding adds nitrogen at lower temperature, and induction or flame hardening heats and quenches the surface.

sections.heading: Choosing a treatment
sections.text: Choose from the required property and section size. Anneal or spheroidise for softness and machinability; normalise for a uniform finer structure; harden and temper for through-hardness; surface harden for a wear-resistant case. Use the iron-carbon diagram to set the austenitising temperature and the CCT diagram to check cooling. Example: cooling from 850 °C to 400 °C in 10 s gives (850 − 400) ÷ 10 = 45 °C/s. If this exceeds the critical cooling rate, martensite is likely. Thick sections cool slowly, so use a more hardenable steel or a faster quench.

keyPoints: The eutectoid steel is about 0.8% carbon at about 727 °C; cooling rate decides whether pearlite, bainite or martensite forms.
Annealing softens and relieves stress; normalising gives a finer pearlite and higher strength.
Hardening forms martensite; tempering below the lower critical temperature trades hardness for toughness.
Austempering holds above the martensite start temperature to form bainite and reduce distortion.
Hardenability is hardening depth, not maximum hardness, and is compared by the Jominy end-quench test.
Average cooling rate = (T1 − T2) ÷ time; compare it with the critical cooling rate from the CCT diagram.

en.title: Nonferrous metallurgy and alloys
en.short: Extraction, refining, properties and main alloys of aluminium, copper, magnesium, titanium, zinc and lead.

sections.heading: Extraction and refining
sections.text:
Nonferrous metals come from oxide or sulphide ores. Aluminium is made by the Bayer process for alumina, then Hall-Héroult electrolysis in molten cryolite. Copper sulphide is smelted, converted and electrorefined. Magnesium is electrolysed from magnesium chloride or made by the Pidgeon process.

Titanium uses the Kroll process, reducing titanium tetrachloride with magnesium. Zinc is roasted, leached and electrowon. Lead ore is sintered, reduced in a blast furnace and refined. Electricity and batch reduction make aluminium, magnesium and titanium costly.

sections.heading: Aluminium and magnesium
sections.text:
Aluminium is light, about one-third the density of steel, corrosion-resistant through a natural oxide film, and a good conductor. Pure metal is soft, so alloys add strength.

2024 (Al-Cu-Mg) has high fatigue strength for aircraft skins; 7075 (Al-Zn-Mg-Cu) is stronger but less corrosion-resistant; 6061 (Al-Mg-Si) is weldable and extrudable for frames. Magnesium is the lightest structural metal. AZ91 (Mg-Al-Zn) die-casts well for housings, but it needs coating because it corrodes easily.

sections.heading: Copper, zinc and lead
sections.text:
Copper conducts heat and electricity very well and resists corrosion. It is soft, so it is alloyed. Brass (Cu-Zn) machines and forms easily, for fittings and cartridges. Bronze (Cu-Sn) is harder and wear-resistant, for bearings and bells. Copper-nickel resists seawater.

Zinc mainly coats steel in galvanising: it corrodes preferentially and protects the steel. Zamak zinc alloys die-cast small parts. Lead alloys with antimony or calcium strengthen battery grids; lead is dense, soft, ductile and acid-resistant, and suits radiation shielding, but toxicity limits many uses.

sections.heading: Titanium and selection
sections.text:
Titanium has a high strength-to-weight ratio and excellent corrosion resistance, but is costly to extract and machine. Ti-6Al-4V (Grade 5) is the main alloy: aluminium stabilises the alpha phase and vanadium the beta phase, giving strength and toughness. It is chosen for aircraft parts, implants and chemical plant.

Comparing metals: aluminium is light and cheap, magnesium is lighter but costs more, and both are limited by strength or corrosion; copper and zinc conduct or protect; titanium performs where cost is justified; lead is chosen for density and acid resistance, not strength.

keyPoints: Aluminium is extracted by Bayer alumina refining and Hall-Héroult electrolysis; titanium by the Kroll process.
Copper is smelted and electrorefined; zinc is roasted, leached and electrowon; lead is sintered and blast-furnace reduced.
Alloying adds strength: 2024 and 7075 aluminium for aircraft, 6061 for weldable frames, AZ91 magnesium for die castings.
Brass (Cu-Zn) machines well, bronze (Cu-Sn) resists wear, and copper-nickel resists seawater.
Zinc protects steel by galvanising; lead is chosen for density and acid resistance but toxicity limits its use.
Ti-6Al-4V combines alpha and beta stabilisers for high strength and toughness in aerospace and implants.

en.title: Solidification and casting quality
en.short: Nucleation, growth, ingot zones, shrinkage, riser sizing, gating and common casting defects.

sections.heading: Nucleation and growth
sections.text:
Solidification begins with nucleation, when atoms form stable clusters. Homogeneous nucleation in the melt needs large undercooling, meaning cooling below the freezing point. Heterogeneous nucleation on mould walls or particles needs less undercooling. Crystals then grow, often as dendrites, tree-like branches along easy growth directions.

Fast cooling gives many nuclei and fine grains; slow cooling gives coarse grains and more time for solute segregation. Grain size affects strength and ductility.

sections.heading: Ingot structure
sections.text:
A chill-cast ingot often has three zones: a thin chill zone of fine equiaxed grains at the cold mould wall; a columnar zone of long grains growing inward along the heat flow; and an equiaxed zone in the hot centre.

High pouring temperature and slow cooling favour columnar growth. Grain refiners and convection favour equiaxed grains. Columnar grains are anisotropic and can trap segregation and porosity between them.

sections.heading: Shrinkage and risers
sections.text:
Metals shrink as liquid, during freezing and in the solid. A riser (feeder) is a reservoir that supplies liquid to the casting as it solidifies; it must freeze after the casting. Chvorinov’s rule estimates freezing time: t = B (V/A)², where V/A is the modulus and B the mould constant, which depends on the metal and mould.

Example: a plate 200 × 100 × 20 mm has V = 400,000 mm³ and A = 52,000 mm², so V/A = 7.69 mm. Taking B = 0.03 min/mm², t = 0.03 × 7.69² ≈ 1.8 min. A riser with V/A = 10 mm takes 3 min, so it freezes later and can feed the plate.

Gating (pouring basin, sprue, runner, ingate) should fill smoothly without turbulence.

sections.heading: Defects and quality
sections.text:
Common defects are shrinkage porosity and pipes, gas porosity, hot tears (cracks while the casting is weak and restrained), misruns and cold shuts from cold or slow metal, inclusions from slag or mould erosion, and segregation.

Quality depends on clean melt, controlled pouring temperature and speed, good mould and gating design, and risers placed at hot spots. Non-destructive testing checks internal soundness.

keyPoints: Solidification starts with nucleation and continues by dendritic growth; faster cooling gives finer grains.
A chill-cast ingot commonly shows chill, columnar and equiaxed zones.
Chvorinov’s rule: t = B (V/A)², where V/A is the casting modulus.
A riser must have a larger modulus than the casting so it freezes later and feeds shrinkage.
Gating should fill the mould smoothly and avoid turbulence and dross.
Shrinkage porosity, hot tears, misruns and inclusions are common casting defects.

en.title: Metal forming and additive manufacturing
en.short: Rolling, forging, extrusion, drawing, sheet forming and powder or wire additive manufacturing.

sections.heading: Bulk forming
sections.text: Rolling passes metal between rolls to reduce thickness. Forging compresses it between dies, extrusion pushes it through a die, and drawing pulls it through a die. All change shape by plastic flow. Rolling draft is Δh = h0 − h1 and true strain is ε = ln(h0 ÷ h1). Example: rolling 20 mm to 15 mm gives draft 5 mm and ε = ln(20 ÷ 15) = 0.288. Friction raises force and makes flow uneven, so surface layers may deform more than the centre and defects such as laps, cracks or voids can form.

sections.heading: Sheet forming
sections.text: Sheet forming bends, stretches or draws flat sheet with a punch and die. The sheet must strain without tearing. Formability depends on material, friction and lubrication, die radius and blank holder force. Too little restraint causes wrinkling; too much causes tearing. Springback, the elastic recovery after unloading, changes final shape and is larger for high-strength metals. Earing, the wavy rim on a drawn cup, comes from crystallographic texture.

sections.heading: Temperature and rate
sections.text: Hot working is above the recrystallisation temperature. It lowers flow stress and allows dynamic recrystallisation, giving equiaxed grains, but oxide scale and poorer finish. Cold working is below it. It strain-hardens the metal, raises strength, leaves residual stress and can produce preferred orientation. Warm working lies between. Higher strain rate raises flow stress and can cause shear bands or cracking. Friction and temperature also affect die wear and defects.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing
sections.text: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model. Powder bed fusion spreads powder and melts selected areas with a laser or electron beam. Directed energy deposition feeds powder or wire into a melt pool. Wire arc additive manufacturing uses an electric arc and wire. Rapid solidification gives fine, often columnar grains along heat flow, so properties are anisotropic. Residual stress, distortion, porosity, lack of fusion and keyhole porosity, where a deep vapour cavity traps gas, are common; heat treatment or hot isostatic pressing may be needed.

keyPoints: Bulk forming changes shape by plastic flow: rolling reduces thickness, forging compresses, extrusion pushes and drawing pulls through a die.
Rolling draft is Δh = h0 − h1 and true strain is ε = ln(h0 ÷ h1); for 20 mm to 15 mm, ε = 0.288.
Hot working lowers flow stress and allows recrystallisation, while cold working strain-hardens and leaves residual stress.
Friction raises forming force and causes uneven flow, which can produce laps, cracks or tears; in sheet forming, too little or too much restraint causes wrinkling or tearing.
Higher strain rate raises flow stress and can cause shear bands or cracking.

Powder bed fusion and wire or powder directed energy deposition build layer by layer; rapid solidification gives anisotropic, often columnar microstructures and defects such as porosity and residual stress.

en.title: Welding and joining
en.short: Fusion and solid-state welding, brazing and soldering, heat-affected zones, weldability and defects.

sections.heading: Fusion welding
sections.text:
Fusion welding melts the edges of the parts, with or without a filler metal, so they join on solidifying. Arc processes such as manual metal arc, MIG/MAG and TIG use an electric arc, and slag or shielding gas protects the molten pool. Laser and electron beam welding give high power density, a narrow weld and a small heat-affected zone.

Case: a workshop in Kano welding a steel tank uses manual metal arc; the electrode coating forms a slag that keeps air away from the cooling metal.

sections.heading: Solid-state welding
sections.text: Solid-state welding joins below the melting point, using pressure, friction or diffusion. Friction welding spins one part against the other, then forges the softened interface. Friction stir welding stirs a non-consumable tool along the seam and is widely used on aluminium. Diffusion bonding holds parts under pressure at high temperature so atoms cross the interface. Because the metal never melts, dissimilar metals and heat-sensitive alloys can be joined with little heat-affected zone.

sections.heading: Brazing and soldering
sections.text: In brazing and soldering only the filler melts; the base metal stays solid. Capillary action draws the filler into a narrow gap, and it bonds by alloying. By convention brazing fillers melt above about 450 °C and soldering fillers below, though the boundary varies between standards. Brazing suits dissimilar metals and thin sections; soldering suits electronics. Clean surfaces, a suitable flux and the correct gap size matter in both.

sections.heading: HAZ, weldability, defects
sections.text: The heat-affected zone (HAZ) is base metal altered by heat but not melted. In steels it may harden and crack. Weldability is the ease of making a sound joint; it depends on composition, thickness and procedure. Common defects are porosity (trapped gas), slag inclusion, lack of fusion, undercut, cracks and distortion. Clean surfaces, correct current, dry electrodes, preheat, post-weld heat treatment and a qualified procedure prevent most of them.

keyPoints: Fusion welding melts the base metal; solid-state welding joins below the melting point using pressure, friction or diffusion.
Brazing and soldering melt only the filler, which is drawn into a narrow gap by capillary action.
The heat-affected zone is unfused base metal changed by the weld thermal cycle.
Weldability depends on composition, thickness and procedure, not on the process alone.
Porosity, slag inclusion, lack of fusion, undercut and cracking are the common defects.
Clean surfaces, dry electrodes, preheat and post-weld heat treatment reduce most weld defects.

en.title: Ceramics and glasses
en.short: Structure, powder processing, sintering, glass formation and the properties of ceramics and glasses.

sections.heading: Bonding and structure
sections.text: Ceramics are inorganic, non-metallic solids. Most have mixed ionic and covalent bonds. These bonds are strong, and the covalent part is directional. Crystalline ceramics such as alumina, Al2O3, have ordered lattices; glasses are amorphous, meaning their atoms lack long-range order. Strong bonds give high melting points, high stiffness and hardness, and low electrical and thermal conductivity. They also leave little room for line defects called dislocations to move, so ceramics do not yield plastically at room temperature.

sections.heading: Powder processing
sections.text: Most bulk ceramics are made from powders. The powder is mixed with additives such as a binder, which gives strength before firing, and a lubricant, then shaped by pressing, extrusion or slip casting, in which a powder suspension is poured into a porous mould. The shaped body is called a green body. Binder burnout removes organics before high-temperature firing.

sections.heading: Sintering and strength
sections.text: Sintering heats the green body below its melting point. Atoms diffuse between touching particles, necks grow, pores shrink and the body densifies. Firing shrinkage must be allowed in the mould. Example: a compact 100.0 mm long fires to 88.0 mm, so linear shrinkage is (100.0 − 88.0) ÷ 100.0 × 100 = 12.0%. For alumina with bulk density 3.78 g/cm³ and theoretical density 3.98 g/cm³, porosity is 1 − 3.78 ÷ 3.98 = 0.050, or 5.0%. Strength is limited by flaws such as pores and cracks, so ceramics are strong in compression but brittle in tension.

sections.heading: Glasses and thermal behaviour
sections.text: Glass forms when a melt is cooled fast enough to avoid crystallisation. Silica, SiO2, is a network former, a glass-building oxide; modifiers such as Na2O break the network and lower the glass transition temperature, Tg, where the liquid stiffens into a glass. Annealing near Tg relieves stresses. Low thermal expansion and good thermal conductivity give good thermal shock resistance, resistance to sudden temperature change, in some glasses and ceramics, but steep thermal gradients can still cause cracking. Applications include tiles, refractories, cutting tools, insulators, implants, containers and windows.

keyPoints: Ceramics have strong ionic and covalent bonds, giving hardness, stiffness and heat resistance but little plastic deformation.
Sintering heats a powder compact below its melting point, bonds particles by diffusion, shrinks pores and densifies the body.
Linear shrinkage = (L0 − Lf) ÷ L0 × 100, where L0 is the original length and Lf the fired length.
Porosity fraction = 1 − bulk density ÷ theoretical density.
Ceramic strength is controlled by flaws, so ceramics are strong in compression and brittle in tension.
Glass is an amorphous solid formed by cooling a melt fast enough to avoid crystallisation; annealing near Tg relieves stresses.

en.title: Polymers and composites: structure, processing and properties
en.short: Polymer structure, molecular weight, crystallinity, processing, properties and composite reinforcement.

sections.heading: Chains and molecular weight
sections.text: Polymers are long molecules built from repeat units. Thermoplastics have separate chains held by weak secondary forces; thermosets are crosslinked networks. Chain length is described by degree of polymerisation, DP, the number of repeat units. Number-average molecular weight is Mn = M0 × DP, where M0 is repeat-unit mass. A wide molecular-weight distribution broadens the glass transition and affects melt flow. Entanglement and van der Waals forces, not just chain chemistry, give strength.

sections.heading: Crystallinity and stiffness
sections.text: Chain regularity allows crystallinity: ordered lamellae mixed with amorphous regions. Crystallinity raises stiffness, strength, density and resistance to solvents, but reduces optical clarity and toughness. Above the glass transition temperature Tg, amorphous regions soften; crystalline regions melt at Tm. Semicrystalline polymers keep stiffness between Tg and Tm. Stiffness depends on chain stiffness, crystallinity and orientation. Drawing aligns chains and raises modulus along the draw direction.

sections.heading: Processing and temperature
sections.text: Processing melts or softens polymer and shapes it: extrusion, injection moulding, blow moulding and compression moulding for thermoplastics; curing for thermosets. Cooling rate controls crystallinity: fast cooling gives finer, less crystalline parts; slow cooling gives more crystallinity and shrinkage. Molecular weight controls melt viscosity; high MW improves toughness but makes processing harder. Service temperature must stay below Tg or Tm, allowing for creep.

sections.heading: Composites
sections.text: Composites combine reinforcement (fibres, particles) with a matrix. Fibres carry load; matrix transfers stress, protects fibres and controls transverse and temperature behaviour. Continuous fibres give high stiffness along fibre direction. The iso-strain rule of mixtures estimates upper-bound modulus: Ec = VfEf + VmEm. Example: Vf=0.6, Ef=200 GPa, Em=3 GPa: Ec=0.6×200+0.4×3=121.2 GPa. Real values are lower because of fibre misalignment, voids and poor bonding. Processing includes hand lay-up, pultrusion and resin transfer moulding. Short fibres and particles give less directional reinforcement.

keyPoints: Number-average molecular weight: Mn = M0 × DP.
Crystallinity raises stiffness and strength but reduces clarity and toughness; Tg marks amorphous softening and Tm crystalline melting.
Cooling rate and molecular weight control crystallinity, shrinkage and melt viscosity.
Composite upper-bound modulus along continuous fibres: Ec = VfEf + VmEm.
Real composite stiffness falls below the rule of mixtures because of voids, misalignment and weak bonding.
Service temperature must remain below Tg or Tm, with creep allowed for.

en.title: Corrosion and degradation of materials
en.short: The corrosion cell, oxidation, passivity, galvanic and localised attack, and prevention methods.

sections.heading: The corrosion cell
sections.text:
Electrochemical corrosion needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metallic path. At the anode the metal oxidises: M → Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻. At the cathode an oxidant accepts electrons, usually dissolved oxygen: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Electrons travel through the metal and ions through the electrolyte. The anode loses metal.

Faraday’s law gives mass loss: m = MIt ÷ (nF), where M is molar mass, I current, t time, n electrons per ion and F = 96 485 C/mol. Example: I = 0.100 A on iron for 30 days gives Q = 0.100 × 2 592 000 = 259 200 C. With n = 2 and M = 55.85 g/mol, m = 55.85 × 259 200 ÷ (2 × 96 485) = 75.0 g.

sections.heading: Oxidation and passivity
sections.text: Dry oxidation is direct reaction with oxygen at high temperature, forming an oxide scale. A dense, adherent, slow-growing oxide protects the metal. Passivity is a thin surface oxide film that greatly lowers corrosion rate; stainless steel relies on a chromium-rich passive film. Chloride can break the film locally and start rapid attack.

sections.heading: Galvanic and localised attack
sections.text: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two different metals touch in an electrolyte. The more active metal becomes the anode and corrodes faster. A small anode joined to a large cathode is especially damaging. Localised attack includes pitting, where the passive film breaks at small spots and deep holes form, and crevice corrosion in shielded gaps.

sections.heading: Prevention choices
sections.text: Prevention starts with materials selection: use a resistant alloy, avoid harmful couples and insulate dissimilar metals. Coatings give a barrier; a sacrificial coating such as zinc on steel also protects exposed areas. Inhibitors are added in small amounts to reduce corrosion rate, but the correct type and dose matter. Cathodic protection makes the structure the cathode, using sacrificial anodes or an impressed current. Good design avoids crevices and trapped water.

keyPoints: An electrochemical corrosion cell needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metallic path.
At the anode metal oxidises; at the cathode oxygen or hydrogen ions are reduced.
Faraday’s law gives mass loss m = MIt ÷ (nF), with F = 96 485 C/mol.
Passivity is a protective surface oxide film; chloride can break it down and cause pitting.
Galvanic corrosion is worst when a small anode is coupled to a large cathode.
Prevention uses resistant materials, coatings, inhibitors and cathodic protection, supported by good design.

en.title: Materials characterisation
en.short: Microscopy, diffraction, spectroscopy and thermal analysis: what each measures and how to read results.

sections.heading: Microscopy
sections.text: Optical microscopy uses visible light. It shows grain size, phase shape, inclusions and coatings. Resolution is limited by light wavelength, about 0.2 µm. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) scans a beam and images surface topography and atomic-number contrast (heavier elements appear brighter); it often carries energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for local composition. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) passes electrons through a thin foil and reveals dislocations, precipitates and defects. Electron methods need vacuum and careful preparation, and can damage samples. EDS is weak for light elements and needs standards.

sections.heading: Diffraction
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) measures angles where X-rays diffract from crystal planes. Bragg law is nλ = 2d sin θ, where d is plane spacing and θ the Bragg angle. Peak positions identify phases and lattice parameters; peak widths give crystallite size and strain. XRD needs crystalline material; peak overlap or preferred orientation can mislead. Amorphous or very thin layers may give little signal. Example: Cu Kα radiation, λ = 0.154 nm, gives a peak at θ = 22.5°. Then d = 0.154 ÷ (2 sin 22.5°) = 0.201 nm.

sections.heading: Spectroscopy and thermal
sections.text: Spectroscopic methods measure composition or bonding. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) gives bulk elemental composition; infrared and Raman spectroscopy give molecular or lattice vibration information; inductively coupled plasma (ICP) methods give trace elements. Results depend on calibration standards, detection limits and sample preparation. Thermal analysis measures change with temperature. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) records mass change, showing moisture, volatiles or decomposition. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) records heat flow, showing melting, crystallisation, glass transition or reaction. Heating rate, atmosphere and sample size affect curves.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: Interpretation combines length scale, composition and phase. A micrograph shows shape and distribution; EDS gives local elements; XRD confirms crystalline phases; thermal analysis shows stability or transitions. No single method is enough. For example, SEM may show a grey inclusion in steel; EDS may show calcium, aluminium and oxygen; XRD can confirm a crystalline calcium aluminate if enough material is present. Report method, conditions and uncertainty; check against standards and references.

keyPoints: Optical microscopy shows microstructure down to about 0.2 µm; SEM shows surface and atomic-number contrast; TEM shows internal defects.
Bragg law nλ = 2d sin θ relates diffraction angle to plane spacing.
XRD identifies crystalline phases and lattice parameters; peak width gives crystallite size and strain.
EDS gives local composition but is weak for light elements and needs standards.
TGA measures mass change and DSC measures heat flow against temperature.
Interpretation needs several methods, because each has resolution, sampling and calibration limits.

en.title: Failure analysis and non-destructive testing
en.short: Systematic failure investigation, fractography, NDT methods and reliability concepts.

sections.heading: Fractography
sections.text: Fractography is the study of fracture surfaces to infer failure mode. Ductile fracture shows dimples and necking; brittle fracture shows cleavage or intergranular paths with little deformation. Fatigue starts at a stress raiser and leaves beach marks, seen by eye, and fine striations, seen by microscope. Preserve and photograph the surface before cleaning.

sections.heading: Root-cause analysis
sections.text: Root-cause analysis is a structured search for physical, human and organisational causes, not only the immediate cause. Preserve evidence, record service history, inspect the site, form hypotheses, then test them with NDT, metallography and mechanical tests. Check design and operation before blaming an operator. Case: a pump shaft broke at a keyway. Dye penetrant found a crack from the sharp corner; fractography showed beach marks. Stress concentration under cyclic load was the root cause; a larger fillet radius and alignment check were the remedy.

sections.heading: NDT methods
sections.text: Non-destructive testing (NDT) inspects a part without damaging it. Visual inspection is the first step: it finds surface damage, misalignment and leaks but not internal defects. Dye penetrant inspection finds surface-breaking defects in non-porous materials: clean, apply penetrant, remove excess, then developer draws it out. Magnetic particle inspection finds surface and near-surface defects in ferromagnetic metals by magnetising the part and applying particles. Ultrasonic testing sends high-frequency sound into the material to find internal defects and measure thickness; it needs a couplant and skill. Radiographic testing uses X-rays or gamma rays to show internal density changes; it needs radiation safety controls. Choose by material, defect type and location, geometry, access, cost and the applicable standard. Standards differ by country and industry, so use the current official one.

sections.heading: Reliability
sections.text: Reliability is the probability that an item performs its required function for a stated time under stated conditions. For a constant failure rate λ, reliability is R = e^(−λt) and mean time between failures is MTBF = 1 ÷ λ. Example: λ = 2 × 10^-6 per hour and t = 10,000 h give λt = 0.02, so R = e^(−0.02) ≈ 0.980. MTBF = 1 ÷ (2 × 10^-6) = 500,000 h. The constant-rate model suits random failures, not wear-out.

keyPoints: Fractography links surface features to failure mode: dimples mean ductile fracture, cleavage or intergranular paths mean brittle fracture, and beach marks or striations indicate fatigue.
A root-cause investigation preserves evidence, tests hypotheses and separates the immediate cause from design, operation and organisational causes.
Dye penetrant finds surface-breaking defects in non-porous materials; magnetic particle inspection is limited to ferromagnetic metals.
Ultrasonic testing finds internal defects and measures thickness; radiographic testing shows internal density changes and needs radiation safety.
Choose an NDT method by material, defect type and location, geometry, access, cost and the current standard, which varies by country and industry.
For constant failure rate λ, R = e^(−λt) and MTBF = 1 ÷ λ; this model suits random failures, not wear-out.

en.title: Materials selection and design
en.short: Structured selection with property charts, performance indices, cost, environment and codes.

sections.heading: Selection process
sections.text:
Define the function, constraints and objective. Function is what the part must do, such as carry a load. Constraints are non-negotiable limits, such as temperature, corrosion resistance or stiffness. The objective is what to minimise or maximise, often mass or cost. Free variables are the open choices.

Screen against constraints, rank survivors by a performance index, then verify materials with stress, fatigue, corrosion, manufacturing and code checks.

sections.heading: Property charts
sections.text:
Property charts plot two properties on logarithmic axes, for example strength against density. Material classes form clusters. A selection line represents a constant performance index; move it until it touches the best cluster to find candidates.

Charts show typical values. Properties vary with grade, heat treatment, temperature and processing, so confirm final choices with supplier data or standards.

sections.heading: Performance index
sections.text:
Example: a tie rod of fixed length L carries force F without yielding. Minimise mass m. Stress σ = F/A, so A = F/σ_y. Then m = A L ρ = F L (ρ/σ_y), so the index is M = σ_y/ρ.

Steel: σ_y = 400 MPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³. Aluminium alloy: σ_y = 300 MPa, ρ = 2,700 kg/m³.
M steel = 400 × 10⁶ ÷ 7,850 = 50,955 m²/s²
M aluminium = 300 × 10⁶ ÷ 2,700 = 111,111 m²/s²
Mass ratio Al ÷ steel = (2,700 ÷ (300 × 10⁶)) ÷ (7,850 ÷ (400 × 10⁶)) = 0.459. Aluminium is 46% of the steel mass.

sections.heading: Cost, environment, codes
sections.text:
Cost and environment are objectives. Cost is mass times price per kilogram; for the tie rod, cost index is σ_y/(cρ), with c the price per kg. Embodied energy, the energy used to produce a material, and carbon footprint are quoted per kilogram, so totals scale with mass; processing and recycling matter.

Standards and codes set minimum requirements and differ by country and use: ISO is international, ASTM is used in the United States, EN in Europe, NIS in Nigeria. Use the project’s adopted edition and check official sources; registration, such as COREN in Nigeria, is separate.

keyPoints: Use a structured process: function, constraints, objective, free variables, screening, ranking and verification.
Performance index for a lightweight tie rod is M = σ_y/ρ, to be maximised.
Mass of a tie rod is m = F L ρ/σ_y, so aluminium alloy can be lighter than steel if yielding governs.
Property charts plot two properties on log axes; selection lines represent constant index.
Cost index for the tie rod is σ_y/(cρ) when minimising material cost.
Standards and codes differ by country and application; use the edition adopted by the project and check current official sources.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and registration
en.short: Ethics, safety, environmental duty, teamwork and engineering registration in different countries.

sections.heading: Ethics and conduct
sections.text:
Professional ethics is the set of duties an engineer owes to the public, employers and the profession. Codes of conduct require honesty, competence, confidentiality and disclosure of conflicts of interest. An engineer must not sign a false report and must report risks to safety. In Nigeria, COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, regulates practice and publishes a code; other countries have their own bodies and codes. Read the current code for where you work.

Case: Aisha, at a foundry in Kano, finds a batch fails a hardness check; asked to release it, she records the result, raises a non-conformance and refuses to sign.

sections.heading: Safety and environment
sections.text: Safety is a professional duty. Engineers assess hazards and reduce risk using the hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, use engineering controls, then administrative controls, and finally personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is the last line. Materials plants bring furnace, dust, fume and chemical hazards. Environmental responsibility means cutting waste, emissions and energy, and considering a product’s life cycle. Rules differ by country; check the regulator.

sections.heading: Teamwork and communication
sections.text: Engineering is teamwork: metallurgists, technicians, designers and managers. Communicate with clear drawings, reports and instructions, and listen to operators. Record decisions and handovers in writing. Explain risk plainly to non-engineers.

sections.heading: Registration
sections.text: Registration recognises that a person may practise as an engineer and protects the public. In Nigeria, COREN registers engineers and regulates practice. South Africa has the Engineering Council of South Africa (ECSA), Kenya has the Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK), and the UK has the Engineering Council with institutions such as the Institute of Materials, Minerals and Mining (IOM3). Requirements usually include an accredited qualification, supervised experience, assessment and continuing professional development (CPD). They differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Professional ethics requires honesty, competence and putting public safety first.
Use the hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administer, then PPE.
Environmental responsibility covers waste, emissions, energy and life cycle.
Good communication means clear records, drawings and plain-language risk explanations.
