Registration bodies such as COREN in Nigeria and ECSA in South Africa set and enforce requirements.
Requirements and codes differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

en.title: Advanced thermodynamics and phase equilibria
en.short: Solution thermodynamics, activity, multicomponent equilibrium, CALPHAD databases and alloy design.

sections.heading: Solution thermodynamics
sections.text: Solution thermodynamics starts from the Gibbs energy of a phase. For an ideal solution, the molar Gibbs energy of mixing is ΔG_mix = RT Σ x_i ln x_i, where x_i is mole fraction and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Real solutions add an excess term, G_ex. A positive excess can cause a miscibility gap; a negative excess stabilises mixing. A regular solution uses G_ex = Ω x_A x_B per mole.

sections.heading: Activity and equilibrium
sections.text: Activity a_i measures the effective concentration of component i relative to its standard state. For a solution, a_i = γ_i x_i, where γ_i is the activity coefficient. The chemical potential is μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln a_i. Phase equilibrium requires equal chemical potential for every component in every coexisting phase. In a multicomponent system this is a constrained Gibbs energy minimisation with mass balance for each element. Example: if x_i = 0.2 and γ_i = 1.5, then a_i = 0.30. At 1000 K, RT ln a_i = 8.314 × 1000 × ln 0.30 = −10.0 kJ/mol.

sections.heading: CALPHAD databases
sections.text: CALPHAD means calculation of phase diagrams. Each phase has a Gibbs energy model with adjustable parameters. Assessors fit these parameters to experimental phase boundaries, calorimetric data and first-principles calculations. The result is a thermodynamic database for a chemical system, such as Al-Cu-Mg. Software minimises total Gibbs energy at each composition and temperature to calculate stable phases, phase fractions and driving forces. A calculated phase diagram is a projection of the database, not a separate empirical drawing.

sections.heading: Alloy design
sections.text: Alloy designers use databases to test compositions. They can calculate stable phases, phase fractions and how the solidification path changes with composition. They can compare driving forces for precipitation or unwanted intermetallics. Results are only as good as the database: extrapolation outside the assessed range, or to a new alloy system, is uncertain and must be checked against experiment. Composition and property limits in design codes differ by country, so check the current national code.

keyPoints: Chemical potential: μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln a_i, with a_i = γ_i x_i.
Ideal mixing: ΔG_mix = RT Σ x_i ln x_i.
Phase equilibrium equalises the chemical potential of each component in all coexisting phases.
CALPHAD builds Gibbs energy models for each phase and fits their parameters to experimental and first-principles data.
A calculated phase diagram is a projection of a thermodynamic database, not an independent measurement.
Database results are reliable only inside the assessed composition and temperature range; check design limits in the current national code.

en.title: Computational materials modelling
en.short: DFT, molecular dynamics and finite element analysis: scales, validation and limits.

sections.heading: Scales and coupling
sections.text:
Materials modelling spans length scales from ångströms (10⁻¹⁰ m) to metres and time scales from femtoseconds (10⁻¹⁵ s) to years. No single method covers all.

Electronic structure methods treat electrons explicitly; atomistic methods treat atoms explicitly; continuum methods average atomic detail into fields such as stress and temperature. Multiscale modelling passes information between them, for example an interatomic potential or defect energy from DFT into MD, or a constitutive law from MD into FEA. The choice depends on the question.

sections.heading: Density functional theory
sections.text:
DFT solves the quantum mechanics of electrons in a periodic solid. It predicts ground-state energies, forces, band structures, defect formation energies and reaction barriers. Accuracy depends on the exchange-correlation functional and pseudopotentials, which must be tested.

Typical cells hold tens to a few hundred atoms over ångströms; ab initio MD runs reach only picoseconds. DFT cannot directly predict a casting defect or a turbine blade stress. Chemical accuracy is not guaranteed; errors vary with the functional.

sections.heading: Molecular dynamics
sections.text:
MD integrates Newton’s equations for atoms using an interatomic potential. It predicts thermal motion, diffusion, dislocation behaviour, fracture initiation and melting at nanometres and nanoseconds. Reactive potentials can model bond breaking; non-reactive potentials cannot.

Accuracy depends on the potential’s transferability to the composition, temperature and phase. Example: a 1 ns run with a 1 fs timestep needs 1 ns ÷ 1 fs = 10⁶ steps. MD cannot reach engineering times without acceleration or coarse-graining, and it does not give electronic structure.

sections.heading: Finite element analysis
sections.text:
FEA solves continuum field equations on a mesh. It predicts stress, strain, heat flow, vibration and deformation of components under loads and boundary conditions.

It needs a constitutive model, such as elasticity or plasticity, and measured or calculated material properties. Results depend on mesh convergence, boundary conditions and assumptions such as isotropy. FEA cannot predict atomistic defects or chemistry; it treats the material as a continuum. Validation against experiment or characterisation is essential. A finer mesh is not automatically more correct.

keyPoints: DFT predicts electronic structure and energies at ångström to nanometre scales; ab initio MD runs reach picoseconds.
MD predicts atomic motion and defects at nanometre to nanosecond scales but depends on the interatomic potential.
FEA predicts continuum stress and heat flow at component scale but needs constitutive laws and validation.
A 1 ns MD run with a 1 fs timestep needs 10⁶ steps.
No model is reliable outside its validated range; compare with experiment or higher-level theory.
Multiscale modelling passes energies, potentials or constitutive laws between methods.

en.title: Advanced electron microscopy and diffraction
en.short: TEM, SEM, EBSD, EDS and EELS: contrast, sample preparation and interpretation.

sections.heading: Electron beams and signals
sections.text: In TEM (transmission electron microscopy) a thin sample is imaged with transmitted electrons. In SEM (scanning electron microscopy) a focused beam scans the surface and collected signals form the image. Secondary electrons show topography. Backscattered electrons show atomic-number contrast. Characteristic X-rays give EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy). Resolution depends on probe size, interaction volume and lens aberrations, not on magnification alone.

sections.heading: Diffraction and contrast
sections.text: Diffraction contrast arises when defects or phases scatter electrons differently. Dislocation lines and bend contours appear. Phase-contrast HRTEM (high-resolution TEM) needs very thin samples and careful defocus. In diffraction mode a parallel beam gives spot patterns; the selected-area aperture limits the diffracting volume. Convergent-beam diffraction gives disks for local symmetry. Bragg law: 2d sinθ = λ. At 200 kV, λ = 0.0251 Å. For d = 2.0 Å, sinθ = 0.0251 ÷ 4.0 = 0.00628, so θ = 0.36°. Camera length calibrates ring radii.

sections.heading: EBSD and spectroscopy
sections.text: EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) indexes Kikuchi bands from backscattered electrons in SEM, usually at about 70° tilt. It maps crystal orientation, grain size, misorientation and texture. EDS identifies elements from X-ray energies but has limited spatial resolution. EELS (electron energy-loss spectroscopy) measures energy loss of transmitted electrons and is sensitive to light elements and bonding. WDS (wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy) gives better peak resolution than EDS.

sections.heading: Samples and interpretation
sections.text: TEM samples must be electron-transparent, often below 100 nm, made by electropolishing, ion milling or a focused ion beam (FIB) lamella. SEM insulators need a conductive coating. EBSD needs a flat, strain-free, clean surface. Interpretation means matching contrast to structure: thickness and bending effects, defect strain fields, and orientation maps. Thickness fringes and bend contours are artefacts, not defects. Calibrate with standards and check for artefacts such as contamination or drift.

keyPoints: TEM images transmitted electrons through a thin foil; SEM scans a probe and collects secondary or backscattered electrons.
Bragg law 2d sinθ = λ relates electron wavelength to diffraction angle; at 200 kV λ = 0.0251 Å.
Diffraction contrast comes from local changes in scattering; thickness fringes and bend contours are artefacts.
EBSD indexes Kikuchi patterns to map orientation, grain size and texture; it needs a tilted, flat, strain-free surface.
EDS gives elemental composition from X-rays; EELS probes light elements and bonding; WDS has better peak resolution.
TEM samples must be electron-transparent, often below 100 nm; SEM insulators need a conductive coating.

en.title: Research methods in materials engineering
en.short: Designing, analysing and reporting a master’s materials research project.

sections.heading: Design and hypothesis
sections.text: Research design is the plan that connects a question to evidence. Start with a focused question, then state a testable hypothesis: a prediction about variables. Define the independent variable you change (for example tempering temperature), the dependent variables you measure (hardness, microstructure), and the controlled variables held constant (composition, specimen size, furnace atmosphere). Include replicates, randomisation, and a control condition. Decide the measurement method and its uncertainty before collecting data.

sections.heading: Literature and planning
sections.text: A literature review is a critical summary of what is known, not a list. Use journal articles, standards and textbooks; record search terms and inclusion rules so the review can be checked. It should show the gap your project addresses and justify your methods. Turn the hypothesis into an experiment plan: specimens, sample size, equipment, calibration, measurement schedule and data sheets. For each test, ask what result would support or contradict the hypothesis. Keep raw data and metadata.

sections.heading: Data and reproducibility
sections.text: Data analysis begins with checking and plotting data. Report the mean and standard deviation, and state the number of replicates n. For readings 210, 214 and 218 HV: mean = (210 + 214 + 218) ÷ 3 = 214 HV; sample standard deviation = √(32 ÷ 2) = 4 HV. The standard error of the mean is 4 ÷ √3 = 2.31 HV. Reproducibility means another researcher can repeat the work from your written method and obtain comparable results. Record every step, keep raw data, and report failed runs. Ethics includes honest reporting, avoiding fabrication or plagiarism, safe handling of materials, and acknowledging collaborators. Rules for hazardous waste and human subjects vary by country; check your local committee.

sections.heading: Dissertation writing
sections.text: Write the dissertation as a structured argument: introduction and gap, aims and hypothesis, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Use figures with units and self-contained captions. Report uncertainty and limitations. Follow your university’s format and citation style; these differ by institution and country.

keyPoints: A research design links a focused question and testable hypothesis to controlled experiments with replicates and a control.
A literature review must show the gap and justify methods, not merely list papers.
Plan specimens, sample size, calibration and data sheets before collecting data.
Report mean, sample standard deviation and n; for 210, 214 and 218 HV the mean is 214 HV and s is 4 HV.
Reproducibility requires a written method, raw data and reporting of failed runs.
Ethics and dissertation format rules vary by institution and country; check local guidance.
